newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia ready to work out future ties with NATO.
newsitem.headline: Russia ready to work out future ties with NATO.

text.p: Russia said on Tuesday it wanted to negotiate a charter governing its future relations with NATO, just hours after the alliance shrugged off protests from Moscow and pressed ahead with plans for eastward expansion.

A NATO official said Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov had asked NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana when Moscow could start the dialogue. Primakov is due to hold substantial talks with the alliance on Wednesday.

NATO foreign ministers had earlier called a special summit in Madrid on July 8-9 to name its first new members from former communist Europe, but sought to deflect Russian anger by pledging not to station nuclear weapons on their territory.
The ministers also agreed to send a new peace force to Bosnia for 18 months and lambasted Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic for failing to respect the results of November's municipal elections.
Russia has long protested that its security would be harmed by NATO's plans to incorporate former Kremlin allies in central and eastern Europe, but the alliance has paid little attention.

"It is interesting that they (the Russians) are now indicating a willingness to talk to us on the essentials. They are no longer asking us to change the enlargement policy before they can talk," said the NATO official.
The alliance devised the idea of a charter with Russia in a bid to reassure Moscow it had no aggressive intentions.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said the ministers had authorised Solana to open negotiations with Russia on a possible charter embracing all aspects of relations between the two former foes.
"The door is open, Russia should walk through it," he told a news conference.
But it could be some time before the start of any NATO-Russia talks, since the alliance has yet to work out exactly what kind of agreement it wants to reach with Moscow.
Defence officials say one possibility would be to form a new structure which might give Moscow a say in running the alliance.

Solana said leaders of the 16-member alliance would gather at a special summit in the Spanish captial to invite certain countries to begin accession talks. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are hot favourites to join first.
They will be the first new members for more than 2-1/2 decades and the goal is for them to win membership in time for the alliance's 50th anniversary in 1999.
Reading from a final communique of the meeting, Solana said the alliance had no plans to station nuclear weapons on the territory of new members.
Shortly before Primakov left Moscow, Russia dismissed suggestions it was softening its opposition as "fantasy".
"We hope we can build on that cooperation on the ground to convince them enlargement is no threat," a NATO envoy said.
"We realise they are in a difficult position. They cannot appear to accept that enlargement is going ahead," he added.
NATO officials stressed that Russia had agreed to take part in a Stabilisation Force (SFOR) taking over from the alliance's current peace-keeping contingent in Bosnia on December 20.
The ministers agreed to send between 25,000 and 30,000 troops to monitor the Balkan state's peace accords next year, but said the force would leave at the end of 18 months.
NATO, which has spent the last year policing the Dayton peace accords on Bosnia, "strongly deplored" Milosevic's cancellation of local election results in Serbia last month.
A NATO statement issued shortly after the start of the meeting also praised the restraint of the Serbian opposition, which has mounted peaceful mass protests against the decision.
